header: Date: 2026-12-22 16:00 PST | Duration: ~78m | Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Ava (Redwood SE), Mike (HelixAI CTO), Priya (Lead ML), Jordan (Infra), Anya (PM)
transcript:
00:00 Samir: okay hi everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Samir from Redwood, with Ava our SE, how's everybody doing?
00:08 Mike: good thanks Samir, excited to dive in, we've been looking forward to the perf talk.
00:15 Ava: hey all, quick agenda, we'll cover runtime perf basics, batching and KV cache, quantization options, then model-specific tuning for Llama/Mistral/Qwen, and MoE routing + RoPE scaling notes; we'll leave time for HelixAI-specific Qs and next steps.
00:35 Priya: sounds good, we care most about p95 latency under 300ms for chat-like workloads, and throughput for bulk embeddings, plus on-prem constraints for customer data.
00:50 Samir: got it, p95 300ms is helpful target, also what's your typical max sequence and average?
00:55 Jordan: average user request 120 tokens, tail up to 2,048 in experiments, but prod we cap 1,024.
01:05 Ava: perfect, that drives kernel selection and cache strategy. quick note: transcription might say rope spelled R-O-P-E sometimes, that's the rotary positional encoding stuff.
01:15 Mike: yeah and we have some MoE experiments, routing costs are a concern, we saw big variance in latency when experts spike.
01:23 Ava: exactly, MoE routing can introduce per-token compute jitter; we'll show batching strategies and routing smoothing.
01:40 Ava: first, runtime throughput: for single-GPU Llama 13B families, continuous batching with dynamic batch sizing gives best average latency; if you force fixed batches you get better throughput but worse p95.
01:58 Priya: when you say continuous batching how do you handle cold-start and KV cache priming?
02:05 Ava: good Q. we maintain prefix-level KV cache; cold requests miss the KV and pay warmup cost, but for chat where history repeats we get high cache hit ratio. We also do partial prefix caching for long contexts to avoid re-compute of early layers.
02:30 Jordan: how big is the cache memory footprint for 1,024 seq at 13B models?
02:36 Ava: ballpark for 13B at float16 the KV for full 1,024 is ~12-18GB of GPU memory depending on head dims and rotary implementation; quantization reduces that but KV remains proportional to seq*hidden.
02:55 Mike: oh that explains some OOMs we saw when batching multiple sessions.
03:02 Ava: one mitigation is shard-by-session KV across GPUs (KV sharding) or keep KV on host with pinned DMA for infrequent accesses, but that impacts latency.
03:20 Samir: we can run a quick comparison — we often suggest KV sharding for Dedicated when tail sequences are common, Hosted uses aggressive prefix caching heuristics.
03:35 Priya: about quantization — we tried q4_0 and q4_f32-like mixes; what's the recommended for preserving generation quality on Qwen-like architectures?
03:45 Ava: Qwen and Mistral have different sensitivity. Qwen seems more robust to 4-bit quantization with q4f32 variants, but Llama heads can see modest degradation in certain language tasks. For you I'd recommend q4f32 for Llama 13B if you need cost reduction but want to keep quality; otherwise q8_0 for safer results. We also support per-layer mixed quantization.
04:12 Mike: do you have numbers for p50/p95 latency with q4 vs fp16 for 13B on A100?
04:20 Ava: rough numbers from our lab: fp16 single-thread gen p50 ~45ms per 64-token batch, p95 ~160ms; q4f32 can drop token compute by 20-30% but memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency shift, so p95 maybe down to ~120ms in ideal pipeline. we'll send exact microbenchmarks.
04:50 Priya: okay interesting. how about for Mistral which is denser?
04:58 Ava: Mistral 7B typically faster per token than wider Llama 13B due to architecture; quantized Mistral in q4 gives large wins, and if you can go to 8-bit weights with activation emulation you'll get good throughput with minimal quality hit.
05:20 Jordan: regarding batching policy, how do you tune concurrency vs batch size to meet latency SLO?
05:28 Ava: we expose dynamic_batching and a max_latency_slo parameter. runtime will grow batches until either you hit SLO or batch cap. For interactive chat you'd pick max_batch 8-16 and SLO 200-300ms; for throughput jobs you can increase batch and accept higher p95. we also do tail-aware scheduling so sessions with long history aren't grouped with short ones.
05:55 Mike: and what about prefix caching TTL? do you evict by LRU or TTL?
06:02 Ava: a mix — LRU for memory pressure and TTL for conversational sessions. you can pin certain system prompts to never evict.
06:15 Priya: RoPE scaling — we've seen hallucination regressions when increasing context; is that RoeP or RoPE micro-behavior?
06:23 Ava: it's RoPE (rotary positional embeddings) scaling issues. when you extend context windows beyond training, standard RoPE extrapolation can degrade. we support RoPE scaling techniques (linear scaling, alpha scaling, and interpolation) and offer a rollback to relative position bias in extreme cases. for Qwen we prefer interpolation + alpha<1.
06:45 Priya: are those kernel-level changes or model patched rewrites?
06:50 Ava: mostly model wrappers and small operator kernels; we have optimized kernels for scaled RoPE for low overhead. but some options require model re-tokenization or small fine-tune.
07:05 Samir: quick interruption — Jordan, for on-prem trying to stay within KMS/HSM constraints, do you have requirements around key ops per second?
07:15 Jordan: we need envelope encryption with HSM and <50ms decryption for session keys, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
07:25 Samir: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault, customer HSM), we can document latencies. we'll include SOC2 artifacts in the security pack.
07:35 Mike: good. next: MoE. Priya mentioned randomized spikes.
07:42 Ava: MoE gating costs: each token goes through a router which selects experts; if you have many experts and uneven routing, you get imbalance leading to hot experts and tail latency spikes. options are: 1) smoothing the router with temperature, 2) capacity factors to limit per-expert queue, 3) routing-aware batching — group tokens by chosen experts before execution.
08:10 Priya: router smoothing reduces specialization though, right?
08:14 Ava: yes it trades off accuracy/specialization for latency stability. you can also hybrid: use MoE for non-latency-critical tasks, or use a distilled dense variant for latency-sensitive queries.
08:30 Mike: how big is the routing overhead in practice? like extra ms per token?
08:35 Ava: router compute is small compared to expert execution for big experts, but the scheduling and memory movement between expert kernels can add tens to hundreds of ms in worst-case. we've seen 2-3x p95 increase if you don't manage routing.
08:55 Jordan: curious about expert sharding across GPUs — does Redwood do cross-GPU collective all-to-all for MoE?
09:03 Ava: we support expert sharding with optimized all-to-all paths using NCCL where available; Dedicated configs can co-locate frequent experts to reduce cross-GPU comms. Hosted optimizes placement heuristically.
09:20 Priya: any recommendations for model selection: Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen for our use-case (chat + code assist + embeddings)?
09:28 Ava: general guidance: Llama family gives strong open-source compatibility and robust instruction tuning; Mistral offers high compute efficiency per parameter, often better latency; Qwen has strong multi-lingual and code behaviors and tolerates quantization well. For mixed chat+code, Qwen or Mistral is often cost-effective; Llama 13B gives good quality but higher memory/RoPE sensitivity.
09:55 Mike: we care about embedding consistency across models for reranking. does Redwood do cross-model embedding alignment?
10:02 Samir: we provide model catalog and can advise on embedding model selection; alignment requires either a supervised re-anchor or a lightweight alignment layer — we can run an eval on your sample set.
10:18 Jordan: on VPC/on-prem deployment — what's the recommended network topology for low-latency access to GPUs in our colo?
10:25 Ava: colocate inference nodes in same rack as HBM backends when possible, use RDMA between GPU nodes for KV sharding, and expose a small set of edge routers in DMZ to handle TLS termination + auth. we'll share topology diagrams.
10:42 Mike: any known issues with private deploy and our SIEM? log volume, retention?
10:48 Samir: retention is configurable; we'd recommend sampling for verbose trace logs and full retention for audit events. we support forwarders to Splunk/Datadog/SIEMs.
11:00 Priya: latency microbench question — how much does token length variance affect batching efficiency?
11:07 Ava: significantly. if you mix 32-token requests with 1,024-token requests, the profiler folds into long-run overhead. We use sequence bucketing to group similar seq lengths and pad minimally; you can also enforce per-route max_seq to keep tails bounded.
11:30 Mike: about rollout strategies — if we pin model versions can Redwood do canary traffic splits by user cohort?
11:36 Samir: yes, we support per-route rollouts, canary by user or percent, and automatic rollback on metric regressions. we also support A/B evals with per-prompt evaluation hooks.
11:52 Priya: during inference, do you recompute rotary embeddings per token or cache precomputed rotations?
11:58 Ava: we precompute rotations for cached prefixes, but new tokens require per-step rotation; our kernels fuse rotation with attention matmul to reduce memory traffic.
12:15 Jordan: is KV cache compressed or quantized when memory constrained?
12:21 Ava: we have experiments with compressed KV (16->8-bit quantized keys/values) which saves memory with some compute cost; it's useful when GPU memory is scarce. we'll share demo numbers.
12:40 Mike: what's the recommended GPU instance for initial pilot — A100 vs H100 vs L40?
12:46 Ava: H100 gives best fp16 throughput and tensor core perf for large models; A100 is cost-effective and stable; L40/RTX class can be used for smaller scale pilots. For quantized inference on 13B, a single H100/A100 with high-memory config is ideal.
13:05 Priya: for on-prem we might prefer A100s for cost predictability. also legal asks for data never leaving VPC.
13:14 Samir: Redwood Private meets that — control plane can be isolated, and we support on-prem management plane if required.
13:25 Mike: back to MoE — you mentioned routing-aware batching groups tokens by expert, but doesn't that increase latency due to reordering?
13:35 Ava: there's an engineering tradeoff. we do intra-batch reordering but maintain per-request ordering semantics via reassembly; it can add small overhead but reduces expert-hot tails; we can also use soft-routing caching where frequent tokens get cached expert outputs.
13:55 Priya: do you support mixed MoE/dense hybrids at inference time?
14:00 Ava: yes, and we often recommend a hybrid where hot paths go to a dense fallback for latency-critical queries and MoE for background heavy-lift tasks.
14:12 Jordan: curious about instrumentation — can we get per-request token-level tracing to understand which tokens hit which experts?
14:20 Samir: yes we can instrument traces with expert routing metadata, subject to retention limits and PII filtering.
14:31 Mike: reminder — our compliance team will want encryption in transit + at-rest, and detailed audit trails.
14:38 Samir: noted, we'll include KMS/HSM integration notes in the security docs.
14:45 Priya: one more on RoPE: we saw soft degradation when extrapolating to 8k context — are there recommended retrain/fine-tune minimal interventions?
14:54 Ava: small fine-tune on extended position indexes with RoPE interpolation often helps; alternatively, linear attention patches or repeating positional patterns can be used. depends on your tolerance for model changes.
15:10 Mike: can Redwood run a benchmark with our sample traffic distribution?
15:15 Samir: yes, send the anonymized traffic histogram and sample prompts, we'll run hosted and dedicated sims and share a comparison.
15:24 Priya: for model selection, can you run cross-model evals on our prompt set (quality + latency + cost)?
15:30 Samir: absolutely, that's part of the pilot scope we proposed.
15:36 Anya: what's the timeline to kick off pilot?
15:40 Samir: we can spin up an initial hosted experiment in 3-5 days once we have samples; on-prem pilot depends on procurement but a week after infra readiness.
15:50 Jordan: procurement note — need SOC2 docs, contract addendum for on-prem licensing.
15:56 Samir: will send security pack and contracting contacts.
16:05 Ava: quick performance summary: 1) Use q4f32 on Qwen and conservative q8 on Llama for balance, 2) KV sharding + prefix caching for long context, 3) routing-aware batching + capacity factor for MoE tails, 4) RoPE scaling via interpolation or small fine-tune for >4k contexts, 5) on-prem topologies with RDMA for KV sharding.
16:30 Priya: that's helpful. any gotchas about model patching when doing RoPE scaling and quantization together?
16:37 Ava: quant + RoPE interplay can expose numeric issues; we recommend validate on held-out evals and run a calibration pass when you quantize after position scaling.
16:54 Mike: thanks, this was great. last question: cost sensitivity — how much does q4 gain actually save per 1M tokens?
17:00 Ava: depends on host pricing but rough hosted numbers: q4 can reduce per-token compute cost 20-40% vs fp16; we have cost spreadsheets we'll share that map directly to your request distribution.
17:15 Samir: ok we'll attach the perf + cost spreadsheet. any final quick Qs?
17:22 Mike: none. thanks all.
17:25 Samir: recap of next steps — Samir sends benchmarks & security pack, Ava prepares runbook and tuning checklist, Jordan supplies traffic histogram. We'll schedule pilot kickoff.
17:36 Priya: thanks everyone.
17:40 Meeting end.
